analysis.one_liner: Replaces the child tax credit and earned income tax credit with a guaranteed monthly payment for every child and small credits for adults.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House committee referral; no vote was ever taken before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap the two main federal tax breaks for families with children — the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit — and replace them with a monthly check for every child under 19, paid directly by the Social Security Administration and sized to close the gap between the poverty line for one person and for two. It would also add a $600 refundable credit for adults aged 19 to 64 and $600 per adult dependent, phasing out at higher incomes. Because the payment would be universal, families with little or no income — who currently get the smallest or nothing from these tax credits — would get the full amount. It was introduced by Rep. Rashida Tlaib with a handful of Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 70 million children in the United States and their families would gain the most: every child under 19 would bring in a monthly payment (about $430 a month per child at current poverty guidelines) regardless of whether the parents work. Families with the lowest incomes — who currently get the least from the child tax credit because they earn too little to qualify — would gain the most, since the payment is universal. Single adults and couples aged 19 to 64 with low incomes and families supporting adult dependents would also receive new $600 refundable credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially the poorest

how_it_helps.text: Every child under 19 living in the U.S. who is a citizen or qualified alien would receive a monthly payment equal to one-twelfth of the gap between the federal poverty guideline for two people and for one person — roughly $430 per child per month.
Unlike today's child tax credit, which requires earned income and phases in with earnings, the payment would be universal: families with no earnings and the lowest earnings would get the full amount.

Adults aged 19 to 64 would get a $600 refundable credit ($1,200 for joint filers), phasing out above $20,000 of income, and households caring for adult dependents over 18 would get $600 per dependent.
Payments would not count as income or resources for any other federal or federally funded benefit program, so receiving them could not cost a family SNAP, housing, or other assistance.

analysis.who_pays: The bill contains no dedicated funding source; it simply appropriates "such sums as are necessary" each year, so the cost — replacing two very large tax credits with an even larger universal program, on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars annually — would fall on federal taxpayers in general, either through borrowing or through taxes set elsewhere. Low-wage workers would also give up the earned income tax credit, which for many is worth more per year than the new $600 adult credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the earned income tax credit, which supplements the wages of low-income workers specifically because they work; replacing it with an unconditional payment would remove that work incentive.

The bill contains no new revenue source — it simply appropriates 'such sums as are necessary' each year — so the hundreds of billions of dollars in annual payments would add to federal deficits or require separate tax increases.

The benefit is capped at the poverty line for a two-person household, so a family with three children receives only about 1.5 times what a family with one child receives, and the payment would not lift a child above the poverty line on its own.

Payments would be automatic unless families affirmatively opt out, which trades take-up for enrollment of families who might not want the program and expands data sharing between the IRS and the Social Security Administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: a guaranteed monthly payment for every child would sharply cut child poverty and would be more predictable and less stigmatizing than today's tax-credit system, which gives the most to families with the highest earnings. The drawbacks are real: replacing the EITC removes a proven work incentive and could reduce employment among low-wage workers, and the new entitlement plus the $600 adult credits would cost on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars a year, requiring either new revenue or deficits. The financing side of the bill is left open, which is a serious design gap. The core tradeoff — cash for families with children, paid for by taxpayers generally — is clear and honest, but the bill as written was never advanced or amended, so it remained a statement of principle rather than a workable law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and nearly two years later it was sent to a subcommittee, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the End Child Poverty Act on April 6, 2023, with two cosponsors at introduction: Rep. Chuy García of Illinois and Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee that handles tax credits.
Over the following months, three additional House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, for a total of five of 216 House Democrats. No Republican cosponsored.
On December 17, 2024, weeks before the Congress ended, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare — a routine step that did not advance it.
The Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or a hearing on the bill, and the House never voted on it. When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one lost anything concrete, but the tens of millions of families who would have received the new child payment are no better off, and the current system of tax credits that delivers the least to the poorest families remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The committee system and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Child Poverty Act and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: 5 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats, and none came from the majority party.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over tax credits
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: House majority leadership in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee agenda and the House floor calendar and never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill sat in committee controlled by the House Republican majority, which took no action on it.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and predatory refund-advance services
industries.note: The earned income tax credit fuels a market for paid tax preparation, refund-advance loans, and high-fee filing products aimed at low-income filers. Replacing the EITC with automatic monthly payments would shrink that market.

The earned income tax credit effectively subsidizes low wages by topping up workers' pay; replacing it with an unconditional child benefit removes part of that support for the low-wage employment model.

Households with children would receive far larger benefits; the cost, in the hundreds of billions annually, would be spread across all federal taxpayers since the bill appropriates necessary sums without a dedicated revenue source.
